findings.problem: The section states the practitioner's per-fill specification as a precondition of every request-based partial fill: quick_review[5] says 'the request-based pathway requires the practitioner to specify per-fill quantities in advance'; orientation[4] says that on the request-based pathway 'the practitioner has work to do first -- specifying the quantity for each partial filling, and capping what a patient may later ask for'; forms_records[1] opens 'On the request-based pathway the practitioner specifies the quantity for each partial filling in advance'.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3) imposes the specification duty only 'Where a practitioner issues a prescription for a schedule II controlled substance and wants the prescription to be partially filled'. Under 1306.13(b)(1)(iii) and (b)(4) the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or a caregiver named in an adult patient's medical power of attorney may request a partial fill with no prior specification, and the (b)(4) cap applies only 'Where a practitioner has requested the partial filling of a prescription in accordance with paragraph (b)(3)'. In Massachusetts, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) and 105 CMR 721.055(A) make the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on the patient's request, again with no specification precondition. Read as written, these three items tell a candidate that a patient-initiated partial fill of a prescription that is silent on partial quantities is unavailable, or must wait for the prescriber -- a wrong answer on Massachusetts facts, and a contradiction of the section's own decision_logic[2], decision_logic[7], role_duties[3] and worked_examples[2].resolution ('right for a prescription the practitioner left unspecified'). Fix: make each statement conditional on the practitioner having requested the partial fill.

findings.rationale: Learning objective 5 asks the candidate to state what each actor must specify in each pathway. Under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3) the prescriber owes the specification only when the prescriber wants the prescription partially filled; on a request by the patient, a minor's parent or guardian, or an MPOA-named caregiver under (b)(4), the prescriber owes nothing, and under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) the Massachusetts lesser-quantity duty on patient request is the pharmacist's. Presenting the specification as a standing prescriber duty on the whole request-based pathway misallocates the actor and makes the patient's route look dependent on prescriber action.

findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(5)(i): where the prescriber requested partial filling when issuing the prescription, the pharmacist notes the quantity dispensed (on the face of the written prescription, in the emergency oral record or in the electronic record) and keeps the dispensing record; the 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' notation with the practitioner's name, date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials applies only to a later consultation-authorized fill; and the '[requester] requested partial fill on [date]' notation with the quantity belongs to (b)(5)(ii) patient-side requests. findings.problem: On the example's own facts (Schedule II prescription from a Rhode Island prescriber, issued six days earlier) the section concludes only that 'The initial partial fill can no longer be made on this prescription', and stresses that the five-day limit 'is the deadline for presenting the prescription for INITIAL partial fill, not the general validity of the prescription'. Read with orientation[2] and quick_review[2], which present the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) 30-day rule as the Massachusetts ceiling 'over all of it', the example invites the conclusion that a full initial fill of this prescription remains available until day 30.
findings.rationale: Unless the Rhode Island prescriber also holds a Massachusetts registration (s. 18(a)), a Schedule II prescription from that prescriber is fillable in Massachusetts only under s. 18(d) (nonnarcotic) or s. 18(d1/2) (narcotic, practitioner registered in Maine or a contiguous state), and each authorizes filling only of prescriptions 'issued within the preceding five days' / 'issued within the preceding 5 days'. On day six no fill of any kind is authorized, partial or full. exceptions[3] may defer the (d)/(d1/2) conditions to the out-of-state section, but a worked example on Massachusetts facts must not point the candidate to general validity where a shorter Massachusetts limit reaches the same facts. Fix: add that, absent a Massachusetts registration, the same facts bar any initial fill after five days under s. 18(d)/(d1/2).

findings.problem: 'Day 30 from 1 March is 31 March. The prescription became invalid on 31 March, eleven days before the request.' Counting 1 March as day 0 (as steps[0] does to reach 'day 42' for 12 April), 31 March is day 30, so the step teaches that the prescription is already invalid on day 30. That contradicts orientation[2] ('on day 31 there is no longer a valid prescription'), common_traps[2] ('invalidated on day 31') and timing_deadlines[6] (the s. 18(d3/4) remainder deadline, which permits day 30, closes 'at the same point the general validity rule closes the prescription'). The arithmetic also slips: 31 March is twelve days before 12 April; eleven matches 1 April.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a): a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 'shall become invalid 30 days after the date of issuance'. Whatever convention the section adopts for the first invalid day, it must use one; as written it teaches both day 30 and day 31, which is exactly the boundary a counting question tests. The example's outcome (day 42) is unaffected.

findings.problem: For 'May the remainder go to a different pharmacy?' the table gives the federal answer 'No restriction stated' and concludes 'Massachusetts, as the only source imposing a restriction'.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.08(e) permits a Schedule II prescription to move between retail pharmacies only as a one-time transfer of an electronic prescription 'for initial dispensing', and 1306.25 confines refill transfers to Schedules III-V. In the preamble to that rule (88 FR 48365, 27 July 2023) DEA states that 'no DEA regulation permits a partially-filled controlled substance prescription to be transferred from one DEA-registered pharmacy to another for dispensing of the remaining portion of the prescription'. Federal law therefore also keeps the remainder at the pharmacy that made the partial fill. The Massachusetts outcome taught (same pharmacy only) is right; the federal column and the 'only source' conclusion are not, and would mislead on a federal-law item.

results.summary: Every field was read and checked against the current text of 21 CFR 1306.08, 1306.12, 1306.13 and 1306.22, M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 18, 22 and 23, 105 CMR 721.055 and 721.020(D)(7), and 88 FR 48365. The core of the section verifies: the no-refill rule; the three federal pathways and their clocks (72 hours from the first partial filling; 30 days from writing, or 72 hours from issue for an emergency oral prescription; up to 60 days from issue unless discontinued); the LTCF and terminal-illness notation, the deemed-violation consequence, the contact-before-filling duty and the four per-fill record elements; the unqualified s. 23(a) 30-day invalidity, with no LTCF or terminal-illness carve-out, overriding the federal 60 days on Massachusetts facts; the mandatory lesser quantity, same-pharmacy, patient-record and 30-day conditions of s. 18(d3/4); the address-triggered five-calendar-day rule in 105 CMR 721.055(A); and the s. 22(c) notation content. All eight mapped practice questions are answerable from the section and none is contradicted. The section cannot be published as it stands. Medium findings: (1) in quick_review[5], orientation[4] and forms_records[1] it presents the prescriber's per-fill specification under 1306.13(b)(3) as a requirement of every request-based partial fill, and as an unconditional prescriber duty in the actor table and role_duties[1]. That duty arises only when the prescriber wants partial filling. Patient-initiated requests, and the Massachusetts mandatory lesser-quantity fill, need no specification. (2) The out-of-state worked example says the five-day limit is 'not the general validity of the prescription' on facts where s. 18(d)/(d1/2) authorize no fill of any kind after five days. Low findings: the federal column says no federal rule restricts which pharmacy dispenses the remainder, but 1306.08(e) and DEA's statement in 88 FR 48365 say otherwise. The first invalid day is given as both day 30 and day 31, and one day count is off by one (eleven for twelve). The (b)(5) notation cases are stated incompletely. The s. 22(c) opioid notation is never assigned to an actor. Criteria that fail through a finding logged under another criterion: paraphrase_fidelity fails through findings 1 and 3, which restate 1306.13(b)(3) without its condition and (b)(5) without its first case, and unsupported_propositions fails through finding 6 (the 'only source imposing a restriction' claim). Each fix is a targeted edit: MINOR_EDIT.

findings.problem: The section teaches that the federal and Massachusetts emergency definitions differ, then tells the candidate to 'read which sovereign the question is asking about' (ma_vs_federal[0]) and to confirm the gate 'on the applicable test' (decision_logic[0]). It never states that a Massachusetts pharmacist dispensing a Schedule II drug on oral authorization must satisfy both. Its main worked example checks only the Massachusetts gate ('Check the Massachusetts gate first ... so this is an Emergency Situation under 105 CMR 721.010'). It never tests the federal elements, and it resolves to dispense.
findings.rationale: 21 CFR 1306.11(a) and (d) permit a pharmacist to dispense a Schedule II drug without a signed prescription only 'In the case of an emergency situation, as defined by the Secretary in § 290.10'. 21 CFR 290.10 requires the prescribing practitioner to determine that immediate administration is necessary, that no appropriate alternative treatment is available (including a drug that is not in Schedule II), and that it is not reasonably possible to provide a written prescription before dispensing. 105 CMR 721.060(B) separately requires a 721.010 Emergency Situation, and 721.060(B)(4) requires the follow-up to comply with federal and state law. On Massachusetts facts both gates bind. Facts that satisfy 721.010 but not 290.10 therefore do not permit oral Schedule II dispensing, for example where an appropriate non-Schedule II alternative exists, or where a written prescription could be provided although an electronic one cannot. The worked example shows the gap. For a patient enrolled in a Medicare-certified or state-licensed hospice program, a faxed written prescription for a Schedule II narcotic serves as the original under 21 CFR 1306.11(g). Massachusetts permits a written, faxed prescription during a temporary technological failure (105 CMR 721.070(A)(2), 721.020(F)(1)). So federal element (c) is not established merely because e-prescribing is down, and element (b) is never addressed. Fix: state that on Massachusetts facts both definitions must be met, and add a federal-gate step to worked_examples[0].

findings.problem: retrieval_prompts[4] asserts that 'Two things must appear on the face of the follow-up prescription' and answers "'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and the date of the oral order". The record table, forms_records[1] and the decision_logic[4] checklist list only those two. The Massachusetts requirement that the follow-up indicate it documents an oral prescription appears only in forms_records[2], and there only as a feature of 'the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) follow-up', a route orientation[2] tells the candidate 'is not the route an emergency oral prescription travels'.
findings.rationale: The section's own Massachusetts route, 105 CMR 721.060(A) to 721.070(B), provides: 'The practitioner shall indicate on the Written Prescription that such Prescription is being issued to document an Oral Prescription'. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) imposes the same indication on an electronic or written follow-up. DPH Circular DCP 19-12-108 states that an emergency oral prescription must be followed 'by a written or electronic prescription for the emergency quantity, including the notation, "Issued to Document an Oral Prescription."', and that 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' is an 'additional notation' for Schedule II. On Massachusetts facts the follow-up therefore carries three face items (with the federal date of the oral order), not two. As written, the retrieval answer key and the checklist teach an incomplete list.

findings.problem: The written-follow-up format rule is stated as 'either transmitted by facsimile or written on a tamper-resistant form; a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled', without adapting it to an emergency Schedule II follow-up.
findings.rationale: 105 CMR 721.020(F) governs written prescriptions only 'where permitted by state and federal law'. For a Schedule II emergency follow-up, both 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) and 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4) contemplate the signed paper prescription 'delivered to the pharmacist in person or by mail'. Under 1306.11(a) a faxed Schedule II prescription is not the original outside 1306.11(e)-(g). Presenting facsimile as an unqualified alternative therefore risks teaching that a faxed follow-up satisfies federal law. 'May not be filled' is also not the operative consequence for a follow-up to a dispensing already made. A follow-up that does not comply with state and federal law has not been delivered 'in accordance with 105 CMR 721.060(B)(4)', and that engages the pharmacist's duty under 721.060(B)(5) to notify the nearest DEA office.

findings.problem: The example treats an oral Schedule IV prescription as a lawful 'general oral-prescription case'. It comes from a practitioner who 'holds no electronic-prescribing exception', and no emergency is claimed ('Ask which route made the oral prescription lawful ... this is the general oral-prescription case'). The resolution then calls the s. 20(c) two-day follow-up 'the default for an oral controlled-substance prescription'.
findings.rationale: Under 105 CMR 721.020(A) every prescription generated in Massachusetts must be electronic 'unless it is a Prescription issued in accordance with an exception listed in 105 CMR 721.070', as the section itself says in orientation[2]. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) bars dispensing a Schedule III-VI substance without an electronic prescription, except as the s. 23(h) exceptions allow. No lawful oral route exists without an exception. The s. 20(c) two-day electronic follow-up is the statutory consequence for such a prescription, not a lawful default route. What 105 CMR 721.070(C) supplies is narrower: a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid oral prescription need not verify its exception status, as steps[2] states correctly. The clock the example reaches is right on the statute's text, but the example teaches that oral controlled-substance prescribing without an exception is a normal Massachusetts route.

results.summary: Every field was read and checked against 21 CFR 290.10 and 1306.11, M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 17, 20 and 23, 105 CMR 721.010, 721.020, 721.040, 721.060 and 721.070 (Mass. Register #1531), and DPH Circular DCP 19-12-108. The section's central deadline teaching verifies. 721.020(A) makes a 721.070 exception the only basis for a non-electronic prescription, and 721.070(A)(4) lists Emergency Situations. 721.060(A) routes emergency prescriptions to 721.070(B): seven business days, or the shorter period federal law requires. DPH's manual confirms that emergency oral prescriptions follow the seven-business-day exception route, not the s. 20(c) two-day electronic default, and the federal seven days in 1306.11(d)(4) is the period that binds. Also verified: the element-by-element comparison of the two definitions; the emergency-period quantity limit, reduction to writing and unknown-prescriber check; the 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and oral-order-date face items; attach and annotate; the postmark rule; the central-fill bar; the DEA-notification duty and its voiding consequence; and 721.070(C). MA-Q-0104 is answerable and uncontradicted. The section cannot be published as it stands. Medium findings: (1) it never states that on Massachusetts facts both emergency definitions must be satisfied. It tells the candidate to pick 'which sovereign the question is asking about', and its main worked example dispenses a Schedule II drug after checking only the Massachusetts gate. (2) Its 'Two things must appear on the face' answer key and checklist omit the Massachusetts indication that the follow-up documents an oral prescription (721.070(B), s. 20(c), DCP 19-12-108). Low findings: the fax and 'may not be filled' framing of the written follow-up, and worked_examples[2] presenting oral prescribing without an exception as a lawful default route. Criteria that fail through a finding logged under another criterion: decision_logic fails through decision_logic[0] (finding 1) and decision_logic[4] (finding 2), and study_usefulness_without_legal_distortion fails through worked_examples[0] (finding 1) and the retrieval_prompts[4] answer key (finding 2). Not treated as defects: the comparison omits 721.010 limb (2), emergencies defined in Department guidance, but no such guidance was identified and DCP 19-12-108 restates limb (1) only. Each fix is a targeted edit: MINOR_EDIT.
